title: Train and Apply a BPE Tokenizer
description: Learn subword merges from a small corpus the way GPT-style tokenizers do, then use them to split new words.
statement:
Byte-pair encoding builds a vocabulary of subwords by repeatedly merging the most common neighbouring pair. Write two functions.

**`train_bpe(corpus, num_merges)`**: `corpus` is a list of words (a word that appears several times in the list counts several times).

- Every word starts as a sequence of its characters.
- A round counts every pair of **adjacent** symbols over all the words (a word counts as often as it is in `corpus`; overlapping positions are all counted, so `"aaa"` has two `("a", "a")` pairs). The pair with the highest count is **merged**: wherever it occurs, scanning each word left to right without overlap, the two symbols are replaced by one symbol, their concatenation. A tie in the count goes to the smallest pair when compared as tuples of strings.
- Do `num_merges` rounds, or stop early when no word has two symbols left. Return the pairs that were merged, in order, as a list of tuples `(left, right)`.

**`bpe_encode(word, merges)`**: split `word` into characters, then apply each merge from `merges` **in order** (each one scanning left to right without overlap) and return the list of tokens.

```python
corpus = ["low"] * 5 + ["lower"] * 2 + ["newest"] * 6 + ["widest"] * 3
merges = train_bpe(corpus, 4)    # [("e", "s"), ("es", "t"), ("l", "o"), ("lo", "w")]
bpe_encode("lowest", merges)     # ["low", "est"]      a word that is not in the corpus, built from pieces that are
bpe_encode("aaa", [("a", "a")])  # ["aa", "a"]
```
tests: assert train_bpe(corpus, 4) == [("e", "s"), ("es", "t"), ("l", "o"), ("lo", "w")], "(e, s) and (s, t) both occur 9 times: the smaller pair first"
assert train_bpe(["aaaa"], 2) == [("a", "a"), ("aa", "aa")], "overlapping pairs are counted; the merge itself does not overlap"
assert train_bpe(["ab"], 5) == [("a", "b")], "it stops when no word has a pair left"
assert train_bpe(["abab", "abab", "cd"], 3) == [("a", "b"), ("ab", "ab"), ("c", "d")], "a repeated word counts every time it is repeated"
assert bpe_encode("newer", merges) == ["n", "ew", "e", "r"], "merges are applied in the order they were learned"
assert bpe_encode("zebra", merges) == ["z", "e", "b", "r", "a"], "characters never seen in training stay single characters"
assert bpe_encode("aaa", [("a", "a")]) == ["aa", "a"], "a merge scans left to right"
assert "".join(bpe_encode("widest", merges)) == "widest", "the tokens always spell the word"
hints: Keep each distinct word as a list of symbols together with how many times it occurs. A helper that merges one pair into a list of symbols will be used by both functions.

Each round: count adjacent pairs weighted by the word's frequency, choose the pair with the highest count, apply the merge to every word. `min` with the key `(-count, pair)` picks the highest count and breaks ties by the smallest pair.
The merge helper must scan left to right and skip past the two symbols it just joined, so that `"aaa"` becomes `["aa", "a"]`. `bpe_encode` applies the merges in the given order, nothing smarter.
explanation:
**The idea.** Start with characters and let the data decide what the vocabulary is: the pair that occurs most often is glued into one new symbol, and the process repeats. Frequent words end up as a single token, rarer ones as a few pieces, and a word never seen before can still be spelled from smaller pieces, so there is no "unknown word". The learned list of merges *is* the tokenizer.

**Applying it.** Encoding replays the merges **in the order they were learned**; applying them in another order gives a different split. That is why the test for `"newer"` is `["n", "ew", "e", "r"]`: the merge `("e", "w")` was learned before any merge could build `"er"`.

**Real tokenizers.** GPT-style models run the same algorithm on *bytes* (so any text, in any language or emoji, can be encoded), first splitting the text with a regular expression into words so merges do not cross word boundaries, with tens of thousands of merges, and an efficient data structure instead of rescanning every word each round. That cost is why vocabulary size is a design decision: more merges give shorter sequences (cheaper attention) but a larger embedding table.

**Complexity.** O(num_merges x total symbols) here.

**Usual mistakes.** Counting each distinct word once instead of by its frequency; letting a merge overlap itself (`"aaa"` with `("a", "a")` gives `["aa", "a"]`, not `["aa", "aa"]`); breaking ties by insertion order, which is not stable; re-deriving `symbols` from the word each round instead of updating them.
